title: Words worth owning
description: Precise words you half-know, pinned down so you can use them with confidence.

ideas.title: Words for how people speak
ideas.summary: English has exact words for speech that is brief, endless, evasive or too smooth to trust.

items.q: Which word, taken from the Greek name for the region around Sparta, means using very few words?
items.a: Laconic

items.q: What does "garrulous" mean?
items.a: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things

items.q: What does it mean to equivocate?
items.a: To use ambiguous language so as to avoid committing yourself or to hide the truth

items.q: A spokesman meets a hard question with a smooth, easy reply that has no real thought behind it. Which four-letter word describes the reply?
items.a: Glib

ideas.title: Words for temperament
ideas.summary: Moods and dispositions have exact names, some of them inherited from the old theory of the four humors.

items.q: What does "sanguine" mean?
items.a: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation

items.q: What does "phlegmatic" mean?
items.a: Calm and unemotional; not easily stirred

items.q: Which word, from the name of a swift Roman god, describes a person whose moods change suddenly and unpredictably?
items.a: Mercurial

items.q: What does "diffident" mean?
items.a: Shy and modest from a lack of self-confidence

items.q: Which word, from the Latin for "even mind", means calmness and composure, especially under strain?
items.a: Equanimity

ideas.title: Pairs people confuse
ideas.summary: Some words are worth owning mainly because they are so often mistaken for a neighbor.

items.q: What does "enervate" mean, a word often mistaken for "energize"?
items.a: To drain of energy; to weaken

items.q: What is the difference between "disinterested" and "uninterested"?
items.a: Disinterested means impartial, having no stake; uninterested means not interested

items.q: What is the difference between "imply" and "infer"?
items.a: A speaker implies (suggests without saying); a listener infers (draws a conclusion)

items.q: What is the difference between "flout" and "flaunt"?
items.a: To flout is to openly disregard a rule; to flaunt is to show something off

items.q: What does "nonplussed" mean in its standard sense?
items.a: So surprised or confused that you do not know how to react

ideas.title: Words for thinking and judging
ideas.summary: Careful thinkers need words for what is unspoken, merely apparent, falsely convincing or sharply seen.

items.q: What does "ostensible" mean?
items.a: Stated or appearing to be so, but perhaps not really so

items.q: What does "tacit" mean?
items.a: Understood or implied without being stated

items.q: A reviewer calls a book's central argument "specious". What is she saying about it?
items.a: That it sounds convincing but is actually wrong

items.q: What does "perspicacious" mean?
items.a: Having keen insight; quick to see and understand

ideas.title: Words for character and conduct
ideas.summary: There are precise words for generosity of spirit and for its opposites, fawning and corruption.

items.q: Which word, built from the Latin for "great" and "soul", describes someone generous and forgiving toward a rival?
items.a: Magnanimous

items.q: What does "obsequious" mean?
items.a: Excessively eager to please or obey; fawning

items.q: What does "venal" mean?
items.a: Open to bribery; willing to act dishonestly for money

ideas.title: Words for beginnings and endings
ideas.summary: Some words fix where a thing stands in its life: just begun, briefly here, or nearly over.

items.q: What does "inchoate" mean, a word sometimes mistaken for "chaotic"?
items.a: Just begun and not yet fully formed

items.q: Which word, from the Greek for "lasting only a day", describes something very short-lived?
items.a: Ephemeral

items.q: What does "moribund" mean?
items.a: At the point of death; in terminal decline
